job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# Drafting Review: S. 2817, Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act (Manager's Amendment, Oct. 6)

I reviewed only the text you provided. I can't browse, so I haven't checked it against current statutes such as the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act of 1980 or the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, or against the bill's status. Have counsel or the committee's staff verify the legal interplay before relying on it.

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A):** The 10,000-ton threshold applies "by a single vessel," so an operator could split recovery across several vessels that each stay below it.
2. **Sec. 2(1)(A):** "Polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources" is undefined, leaving unclear whether cobalt crusts, seafloor massive sulfides, or sediment-based resources are covered.
3. **Sec. 2(1)(A):** It is unclear whether the 10,000 metric tons counts dry or wet weight, and whether tailings or discarded sediment count toward it.
4. **Sec. 2(1)(A):** The 200-meter depth threshold is not tied to any location or jurisdiction, so it's unclear whether shallower seabed or areas beyond U.S. jurisdiction are covered.
5. **Sec. 2(1)(B):** "The Secretary" is undefined (Commerce? Interior? State?), and no process, standard, notice, or record is specified for the "comparable risk" determination. That makes it both hard to administer and easy to challenge under the APA as arbitrary.
6. **Sec. 2(1)(B):** "Comparable" to activities in (A) is not defined, and (A) is measured by tonnage, so the two prongs don't align.
7. **Sec. 2(2):** "U.S. person" excludes LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and other non-corporate entities, and "State" is undefined, so it's unclear whether D.C. and the territories are included.
8. **Sec. 2(3):** The 5,000-gross-ton threshold for "covered vessel" and the undefined term "equipped for the recovery" mean smaller vessels that still exceed the Sec. 2(1)(A) threshold could operate outside the registry.
9. **Sec. 3(a):** The prohibition doesn't reach processing, financing, equipment supply, or importing minerals recovered abroad, so the economic chain could continue even with the mining ban in place.
10. **Sec. 3(a):** Extraterritorial reach is limited to "any U.S. person anywhere." Foreign-flagged vessels and foreign companies operating outside U.S. jurisdiction are not addressed, and "United States" is undefined (it doesn't say whether the EEZ or continental shelf is included).
11. **Sec. 3(b):** "Exploration license" is undefined, and the bill doesn't say which agency issues such licenses or how it relates to existing permitting under the 1980 Act. It's unclear whether it covers only exploration or any mining done under the license.
12. **Sec. 3(b):** The grandfather clause is keyed to enactment, not the Sec. 8 effective date. Licenses could be issued during the 180-day gap and then cover commercial mining with no volume cap, time limit, or transfer restriction.
13. **Sec. 3(c):** "Environmental assessment" is undefined, and there are no limits on volume, duration, sale of recovered minerals, or required approvals. The "for the purpose of" test is also hard to prove, which makes this a broad exemption.
14. **Sec. 4 (no penalty):** Neither the registration (4(a)) nor the quarterly reporting (4(b)) requirement has its own penalty, and Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3. These obligations are effectively unenforceable as written.
15. **Sec. 4(a)–(b):** There's no registration deadline, "operator" is undefined, and the reports have no content requirements (tonnage, location, depth, byproducts). Certification has no standard, and the reports aren't required to be published or reviewed.
16. **Sec. 5 (enforcement machinery):** No agency is designated to enforce, and there are no procedures for assessment, hearings, judicial action, injunctions, or vessel seizure or forfeiture.
17. **Sec. 5(a):** "Violation" and "each day" are undefined, so it's unclear whether penalties run per vessel, per ton, or per day, and there's no inflation adjustment or limitations period.
18. **Sec. 5(b):** "Willfully" is undefined, and there's no responsible-corporate-officer provision, which makes individual liability uncertain.
19. **Sec. 5(a) vs. Sec. 8 (internal conflict):** Penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the prohibition takes effect 180 days later. It's unclear whether any conduct during that window is penalized.
20. **Sec. 6:** "Shall seek to negotiate" creates no obligation with real consequence, and "prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3" is undefined. The section doesn't address interaction with the International Seabed Authority or UNCLOS, or whether the Act lapses if an agreement is reached.
21. **Sec. 7(a):** "Serious harm" is undefined, and no deadline is set for the NASEM report, so the prohibition could persist indefinitely if no report issues. It's also unclear whether a joint resolution "finding" actually lifts the prohibition or only records a finding, and whether it must be presented to the President.
22. **Sec. 7(a) vs. Sec. 7(b) (internal conflict):** Sec. 7(a) says the prohibition "remains in effect" until a joint resolution, while Sec. 7(b) says the entire Act "shall cease to have effect" after 10 years, which would end the prohibition regardless of the NASEM finding.
23. **Sec. 7(b):** The sunset has no savings clause, so it's unclear whether violations committed before the sunset can still be prosecuted or penalized.
24. **General:** There's no severability clause, so a court striking one provision (for example, the vague Sec. 2(1)(B)) could affect the whole structure. There's also no preemption or savings clause addressing existing permits under the 1980 Act.

**Highest priority for the markup:** Items 19 and 22 (internal contradictions), 14 (unenforceable registry and reporting), 12 (enactment-date grandfathering), 13 (broad environmental-assessment exemption), and 1 (single-vessel threshold).
